title: Subtones, the Selmer saxophone and Merle's advice
summary: Thomas explains Jacobson's subtones, keeping one embouchure across registers, why Selmers carry, and Merle's saying that sound comes from the way you blow.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: He told you he invented subtones, huh?

Yes. He could play subtones all the way up to High-F. And most guys on tenor just play subtones in the lower register; they didn't bother about playing subtones in the upper register. But the secret was... Do you know the secret of playing subtones? Just keep the tongue close to the reed. That subdues it and don't let it vibrate so much. And just keep it close to the reed(?)... And sure enough, you can go... Merle always showed me how you don't have to change your embrochure from one register to another. You just play with the same embrochure. You can play with a B-flat the same as you play a High-F. It ain't no difference if you're blowing right. Because the horn, Selmer horn is built in tune.
Well, I heard that it was the best horn made. And you know the secret about Selmer. Selmer didn't put no key on the... I don't know how to say it...

...the body of the instrument. They always put a plate on there, and then put the key on the plate. So a Selmer horn carries. Because Merle told me when I studied, he said, 'Guys are going to come up to you and ask you what kind of mouthpiece you're playing, what kind of reed you're playing -- but it's going to be the way you're
blowing." And sure enough, it happened.
